keyVerseText: And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed. Noah: Gr. Noe: that is Rest, or, Comfort
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb נָחַם (nâcham) is a primitive root that fundamentally conveys the act of breathing deeply or sighing, which metaphorically extends to feelings of sorrow, repentance, and comfort. This literal sense of a deep breath or sigh enriches the common English translations by highlighting an inward emotional response—whether it be regret, consolation, or compassion—rather than merely an external action. Thus, the root sense captures both the physical expression and the internal experience of change or relief.
usageInScripture: With 108 occurrences, נָחַם is used primarily to express repentance and comfort, appearing most frequently in forms translated as 'repented' (10 times) and 'to comfort' (6 times). The word also appears in reflexive forms such as 'to be comforted' and 'comforters,' showing its flexibility in conveying both self-directed and other-directed emotional states. This range reveals a consistent theological emphasis on God’s and humans’ capacity to experience sorrow, change of heart, and consolation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding נָחַם is vital for grasping the biblical narrative of repentance and divine compassion. The word encapsulates both human sorrow over sin and the comforting mercy of God, illustrating how repentance is not merely regret but a transformative turning toward grace. This dual aspect underscores the gospel message: God’s invitation to repent is also an invitation to be comforted and restored. Recognizing the depth of this term enriches faith by emphasizing that God’s dealings with humanity engage both justice and tender compassion.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 5:29 states, 'And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.' Here, נָחַם highlights the hope that Noah embodies as one who will bring relief and consolation amid the curse on the earth. The word’s meaning of comforting deeply connects with the promise that through Noah, God’s people will find respite and restoration from hardship, pointing forward to God’s redemptive purposes.
